answer.label: Not Douglas MacArthur — actually Oliver P. Smith
answer.authorDates: 1893–1977 · U.S. Marine Corps general, commander of the 1st Marine Division in Korea
answer.sourceLine: The line belongs to Maj. Gen. Oliver P. Smith, who pulled his 1st Marine Division out of the Chosin Reservoir in December 1950. TIME’s 18 December 1950 issue quoted him: “Retreat, hell! … We’re not retreating, we’re just advancing in a different direction.” Marine accounts give “attacking in another direction.” The popular “We are not retreating, we are advancing in another direction” is a reworded form, and Sarah Palin credited it to MacArthur in 2009.

source.heading: Where the words actually appear

docMeta.dd: Maj. Gen. Oliver P. Smith, USMC

source.excerpt: “Retreat, hell!” snapped Major General Oliver Prince Smith, commander of the 1st Marine Division … “We’re not retreating, we’re just advancing in a different direction.”
trail: December 1950: TIME’s report on the Chosin breakout quotes Smith as saying “We’re not retreating, we’re just advancing in a different direction” (TIME, 18 Dec 1950 ↗).
1955: TIME’s profile of Smith gives the line as “Retreat, hell! … We’re just attacking in a different direction” (TIME, “Warrior,” 12 Sept 1955 ↗).

Wikiquote records Smith’s version as “Retreat Hell! We’re just attacking in another direction,” said in December 1950 (Wikiquote: Oliver P. Smith ↗). Wikipedia calls the “advancing in a different direction” wording a common misquote (Wikipedia ↗).

July 2009: Sarah Palin ends her resignation speech with “In the words of General MacArthur said, ‘We are not retreating. We are advancing in another direction’”. Critics pointed out it was Smith’s line (History News Network ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the press version. Accounts from the Marines give it as “attacking in another direction.” A 2019 Marine Corps Gazette article says that at Hagaru-ri, Smith told correspondents: “Gentlemen we are not retreating. We are merely attacking in another direction.” None of these versions names MacArthur.

sourceLink.text: TIME, “Retreat of the 20,000” (18 Dec 1950), Wayback Machine copy

source.rightsNote: The popular wording is a reworded form with no single source, so quotle.info claims no copyright status for it. The closest printed version appeared in TIME on 18 December 1950. That is a 1931-or-later publication, so it should not be treated as public domain.

author.name: Oliver P. Smith
author.heading: About Oliver P. Smith
author.bio: Oliver Prince Smith commanded the 1st Marine Division in the first year of the Korean War. That included the Battle of Chosin Reservoir, where his surrounded division fought its way out to the sea. He was a quiet, studious officer whose Marines called him “the Professor,” and he retired as a four-star general.

misattribution.heading: Why MacArthur gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The “not retreating” quip comes from the Marines’ fighting withdrawal from the Chosin Reservoir in 1950. MacArthur was the overall commander in Korea at the time, which makes him an easy name to reach for. But none of the sources tie the words to him.

items.why: Sarah Palin closed her July 2009 resignation speech with “In the words of General MacArthur said, ‘We are not retreating. We are advancing in another direction.’” History News Network called it a misattributed misquotation and traced it to Marine Gen. Oliver P. Smith at Chosin (HNN, July 2009 ↗).
Some commentators went along with Palin’s attribution. The Spectator’s Alex Massie described her as quoting “General Douglas MacArthur’s absurd line” (The Spectator, 3 July 2009 ↗).

items.who: Oliver P. Smith, as worded by the press
items.why: TIME printed “advancing in a different direction” in 1950 (TIME ↗). Marine sources say “attacking,” and one account says Smith later remarked that he had not put it quite that colorfully (19FortyFive ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Maj. Gen. Oliver P. Smith’s, from the Chosin Reservoir in December 1950. The best-attested wording is “attacking in another direction” (Wikiquote ↗); the “advancing” form comes from the press (TIME, 1950 ↗; Wikipedia ↗).

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: In late 1950, Chinese forces surrounded the 1st Marine Division at the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea. Smith led a fighting breakout toward the coast. Because Chinese troops were blocking the way in every direction, he argued that the move was an attack, not a retreat. His answer to correspondents became one of the best-known lines of the Korean War. A 1952 film took its title, Retreat, Hell!, from it.

Dropping Smith’s name turned it into an all-purpose line for putting a good face on a setback. That is how it ended up credited to the war’s most famous general when Sarah Palin used it to explain leaving office.
context.detailsSummary: Which wording is closest to Smith?
detailsBody: A 2019 article in the Marine Corps Gazette says Smith spoke at Hagaru-ri, telling correspondents: “Gentlemen we are not retreating. We are merely attacking in another direction” (Marine Corps Gazette, Nov 2019 ↗).
The punchier “Retreat, hell!” opening and the verb “advancing” both appear in TIME’s December 1950 report. Neither appears in that Marine account.
